title: Validate a BST

why_it_exists.problem: Checking if a tree is a valid Binary Search Tree is notoriously tricky because simply checking if the left child is smaller and the right child is larger is insufficient. A node deep in the left subtree might accidentally be larger than the absolute root.
why_it_exists.better_idea: You must enforce the invariant globally by passing a dynamically shrinking valid range (a `min` and `max` bound) downwards during a pre-order traversal, or by ensuring an in-order traversal yields a strictly increasing sequence.

mental_model.intuition: Every node acts as an enforcer, passing stricter and stricter boundary laws down to its children.
mental_model.description: The root starts with permission to be any value [-inf, inf]. When recursing left, the parent imposes a new maximum limit (the parent's value). When recursing right, the parent imposes a new minimum limit. If any node steps outside its inherited bounds, the tree is invalid.
mental_model.repeated_decision: Does my value fit inside the absolute [min, max] bounds inherited from my ancestors?

explanation:
The 'local check trap' is the most famous failure mode here. Imagine a root `[10]`, with a left child `[5]`, and that left child has a right child `[12]`. Locally, `[12]` is correctly greater than `[5]`. But globally, it fails, because it is in the left subtree of `[10]` and must therefore be strictly less than 10.

To solve this using the top-down (pre-order) approach, pass `min_val` and `max_val` down the call stack. Initialize them to negative and positive infinity. At node `N`, you verify `min_val < N.val < max_val`. Then, when calling `validate(node.left)`, you pass `N.val` as the new `max_val`. When calling `validate(node.right)`, you pass `N.val` as the new `min_val`.

Alternatively, you can use the in-order approach: since an in-order traversal of a valid BST must produce a strictly ascending sorted list, you can just traverse in-order, keeping track of the previously visited value. If you ever visit a node whose value is less than or equal to the previous value, the tree is invalid.

key_points.title: Global bounds
key_points.detail: A node is constrained not just by its immediate parent, but by every ancestor above it. You must pass boundary limits downwards.

key_points.title: In-order alternative
key_points.detail: If you struggle with bounds, remember that in-order traversal on a BST yields sorted order. You only need a pointer to track `prev_val`.

common_mistakes.title: The local check trap
common_mistakes.explanation: Writing `return node.left.val < node.val and node.right.val > node.val`. This only checks the immediate children and fails to catch global invariant violations deeper in the tree.

common_mistakes.title: Failing on duplicate values
common_mistakes.explanation: If a BST definition strictly requires left < parent < right, then duplicate values are invalid. Make sure you use strictly less/greater bounds (`<` and `>`), not less-than-or-equal (`<=`).

recall_questions.q: Why is it insufficient to just verify that a node is larger than its left child and smaller than its right child?
recall_questions.answer: Because it fails to enforce global constraints. A node deep in the left subtree of the root might have a right child that is technically larger than its immediate parent, but illegally larger than the root itself.

recall_questions.q: If you use a top-down boundary approach, what bounds are passed when recursing to the left child?
recall_questions.answer: The `min_val` bound remains unchanged, but the `max_val` bound is updated to be the parent node's value.

recall_questions.q: How can you validate a BST using an in-order traversal?
recall_questions.answer: Track the previously visited value during an in-order traversal. If the current node's value is ever less than or equal to the previous value, the BST is invalid.

oa_questions.question: Validate if a given binary tree is a valid binary search tree (BST).
oa_questions.answer: Implement a helper function `isValid(node, lower_bound, upper_bound)`. If node is null, return true. If `node.val <= lower` or `node.val >= upper`, return false. Return `isValid(node.left, lower, node.val)` AND `isValid(node.right, node.val, upper)`.
oa_questions.approach: This is the classic, O(n) time, O(h) space top-down boundary enforcement.

oa_questions.question: Can you validate a BST in O(1) space? (Ignoring the call stack)
oa_questions.answer: Yes, use an iterative in-order traversal tracking only a single `prev` variable to compare against the current node.
oa_questions.approach: Identify that the in-order invariant guarantees sorted output, requiring only O(1) auxiliary state.

engineering_examples.title: Data Integrity Constraints
engineering_examples.problem: Ensuring a serialized tree uploaded by a user is structurally sound before processing it.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Validating the structural invariants of inputs is a critical security and stability measure before feeding foreign data into your internal systems.
